question: What becomes possible once a product range is highly standardised?

answer.answer:
The question's "highly standardised product range" matches the attribute Highly standardised (AT7) directly, so nothing is widened here. Standardising the range opens six cited routes and underwrites a seventh: an interchangeable kit-of-parts configurator (AR6), modular architecture (AT2), design for manufacture and assembly (PR9), robotic assembly (PR4), lower construction complexity (VA7), the ability to absorb late design changes (VA21), and industrialised scale (AT8), which cannot be reached without it. The set is not flat: the route to lower complexity is carried by 15 of the 50 coded cases and the one to late design changes by only 2, and that second claim is softened in its own source, so treat flexibility as the least supported promise of standardisation. Note also that standardisation and modularity feed each other rather than running one way, and that no deployed project record in front of me exercises any of these paths, so this rests on the literature and the coded counts.

**What standardisation makes possible**

AT7 "Highly standardised" (Attribute) is one of the better represented enablers in the record: 25 of the 50 coded cases draw on it [1], and it carries 2 inbound and 6 outbound dependency edges, all of which are listed in the context [1], so the routes below are the complete cited set.

The outbound routes, with how many of the 50 cases carry each edge (that is, draw on both ends):

- Kit-of-parts. AT7 enablesCapability AR6 "Configurators/kit-of-parts", on standards-grade evidence, carried by 11 of the 50 coded cases [1], on the ground that modular coordination permits the interchangeability of different components [1]. AR6 in turn enables PR11 "Mass-customisation" (carried by 9 of the 50), because the design configurator integrates customisation data into robotic manufacturing [1], which is the practical payoff: variety out of a fixed catalogue.
- Modular architecture. AT7 enables AT2 "Modular", on the argument that decoupled standardised interfaces enable modular architecture and component interchange [2], peer-reviewed and carried by 11 of the 50 [1].
- DfMA. AT7 enables PR9 "DfMA for DFAB process", carried by 13 of the 50, on the finding that design standardisation and simplification is a DfMA enabler for offsite construction [1].
- Robotic assembly. AT7 enables PR4 "Robotic assembly", carried by 10 of the 50, because Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [1]. PR4 itself is drawn on by 13 of the 50 [1], so nearly every case that assembles robotically also standardises.
- Reduced complexity. AT7 enables VA7 "Reduce construction complexity" on standards-grade evidence: the base module standard reduces component variety and coordinates design, manufacture and assembly [3], carried by 15 of the 50 [1], the strongest of AT7's own outbound routes.
- Late design changes. AT7 enables VA21 "Accommodate late design changes", peer-reviewed, but the source is a terminological review and the claim is recorded as softened: standardisation of interfaces supports interchangeability and system flexibility [4]. The edge is carried by 2 of the 50 [1] and VA21 is drawn on by 3 of the 50 in its own right [1]. Of AT7's own outbound routes this is the thinnest by an order of magnitude against the complexity route, and it is the one to be most careful with in an argument to a client.

**The route that requires standardisation rather than following from it**

AT8 "Industrialised" dependsOn AT7: industrialised-construction scale depends on standardisation [5], carried by 16 of the 50, the most-carried of all AT7's edges [1]. Read directionally, AT7 is the requirement and AT8 the consequence, so industrialised scale belongs with the list above: it is what standardisation buys. AT8 is drawn on by 23 of the 50 [1], and it carries its own consequences and conditions: AT8 enables VA3 "Improve quality/performance", carried by 22 of the 50, on the finding that quality-oriented industrialised production considerably increases housing quality by providing standard fittings [1], while AT8 dependsOn RI12 "Delivery/business model/work culture", carried by 13 of the 50: adoption at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [1]. So the organisational change sits upstream of the scale, not after it.

**The loop back**

Standardisation is not a starting point. AT2 "Modular" enables AT7, because modular architecture reduces the variety of component sizes produced [6], carried by 11 of the 50 [1], the mirror of DEP53. Modularity and standardisation reinforce each other, and the record carries the pair in both directions at equal weight.

**Limits of this answer**

AT7 applies in the Design phase with a span across all phases [7], which fits a decision taken once at product-range level and paid off downstream. The retrieved context carries no deployed process record, no census record and no named firm against any of these edges, so I cannot point you to a project that exercised them; the support here is the coded counts across the 50 cases plus peer-reviewed and standards-grade literature. Finally, the cited dependency layer is sparse, touching 68 of the 140 enablers, and an enabler with no edge is still present and usable, its evidence being how many of the 50 cases draw on it [1], so the seven routes above are what the literature has connected to standardisation, not the whole of what standardisation travels with.
